lessons.title: Rank Documents by Similarity
lessons.summary: Score every document, sort descending, and return an explicit top-k result contract.

contentBlocks.text: Keep identity attached to score

A retrieval result should carry document ID, score, and usually source metadata. Sorting descending places strongest similarity first, while deterministic tie-breaking makes tests and pagination stable.

ranked = sorted(scored, key=lambda item: (-item["score"], item["id"]))
return ranked[:k]

challenge.instructions: Given documents and a score function, attach scores, sort highest first, and return k items.
challenge.starterCode:
def top_k(query, documents, score_fn, k):
    scored = []
    for document in documents:
        score = score_fn(query, document["vector"])
        scored.append({"id": document["id"], "score": score})
    ranked = ____
    return ____
challenge.solution:
def top_k(query, documents, score_fn, k):
    scored = []
    for document in documents:
        score = score_fn(query, document["vector"])
        scored.append({"id": document["id"], "score": score})
    ranked = sorted(scored, key=lambda item: (-item["score"], item["id"]))
    return ranked[:k]
challenge.explanation: Negative score produces descending order while ID provides a deterministic secondary key; slicing enforces k.
hints: Sort by negative score and then ID.
Slice ranked from the start through k.

lessons.title: Combine Lexical and Semantic Search
lessons.summary: Use exact-term strength and semantic recall together through rank fusion or calibrated scores.

contentBlocks.text: Keywords and meaning fail differently

Lexical search excels at exact identifiers, product codes, names, and rare terms. Semantic search handles paraphrase and conceptual similarity. Hybrid retrieval collects candidates from both and fuses their ranks before optional reranking.
Raw lexical and vector scores live on different scales; rank fusion avoids pretending they are directly comparable without calibration.

challenge.instructions: Users search both exact error code E1042 and natural-language descriptions. Choose the strongest design.

choices.text: Retrieve lexical and vector candidates, fuse ranks, then rerank the combined set.
Use vectors only and discard exact codes.
Use character count as the only rank signal.

challenge.explanation: Lexical retrieval preserves exact identifiers while vector retrieval catches paraphrases; fusion uses their complementary strengths.
hints: One query type is exact; the other is semantic.
Preserve candidates from both signals.

lessons.title: Evaluate Retrieval before Generation
lessons.summary: Measure whether known relevant sources are present in the candidate set.

contentBlocks.text: Retrieval needs its own ground truth

For labeled queries, recall@k measures the share of relevant documents appearing in the top k. Mean reciprocal rank rewards placing the first relevant result early. Slice results by query type, language, and source freshness to uncover uneven behavior.
If the needed evidence is absent, generation cannot cite it reliably. Diagnose retrieval separately from answer generation.

challenge.instructions: A query has two known relevant documents; the top three results contain one. What is recall@3?
challenge.explanation: One of two relevant documents was retrieved, so recall is 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5.
hints: Count retrieved relevant items.
Divide by all known relevant items.

courses.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
courses.summary: Build grounded answer systems from document ingestion through retrieval, citations, abstention, and component-level evaluation.

modules.title: Ingest and Retrieve Evidence
modules.summary: Transform source documents into traceable chunks and retrieve evidence suited to the user’s question.

lessons.title: Ground Answers in Retrieved Evidence
lessons.summary: Understand RAG as an evidence pipeline rather than a way to retrain model knowledge.

contentBlocks.text: Retrieve first, generate second

RAG searches an external collection at request time and places selected passages into model context. It is useful for private, changing, or source-cited knowledge because documents can be updated independently of model weights.
The grounded loop
items: Interpret the question.
Retrieve candidate evidence.
Rerank and assemble context.
Generate within evidence boundaries.
Return citations and confidence signals.

challenge.instructions: Explain why a policy assistant should retrieve the current handbook rather than rely only on model pretraining.
challenge.explanation: Retrieval supplies the latest controlled source at request time and makes citations possible; pretrained knowledge may be old, absent, or impossible to audit.
hints: Policy versions change after model training.
The answer should point back to an authoritative source.

lessons.title: Chunk around Meaningful Units
lessons.summary: Balance retrievability, self-contained meaning, and context efficiency when splitting documents.

contentBlocks.text: A chunk is the unit the retriever can find

Chunks that are too large mix unrelated topics and waste context. Chunks that are too small lose definitions and qualifications. Prefer headings, paragraphs, procedures, and table rows as semantic boundaries, then test sizes on real questions.
Overlap can preserve sentences crossing a boundary, but excessive overlap duplicates results and crowds the context with near-copies.

challenge.instructions: A five-step incident procedure has warnings attached to steps 2 and 4. Which chunking rule is strongest?

choices.text: Keep each procedure section with its steps and associated warnings.
Split every fixed 20 characters regardless of sentence boundaries.
Put the entire handbook in one chunk.

challenge.explanation: Semantic sections preserve the relationship between actions and warnings while remaining focused enough to retrieve.
hints: A retrieved chunk should make sense on its own.
Do not separate a warning from the step it qualifies.

lessons.title: Create Overlapping Word Chunks
lessons.summary: Implement a transparent chunker with validated size and overlap invariants.

contentBlocks.text: Advance by size minus overlap

A simple word chunker is not production-grade semantic parsing, but it makes the mechanics visible. The step must be positive, so overlap must be smaller than chunk size; the final slice naturally contains fewer words.

challenge.instructions: Validate overlap, advance by chunk_size - overlap, and join each slice into text.
challenge.explanation: The positive step controls repeated boundary words, and slicing safely handles the shorter final chunk.
hints: Step is chunk_size minus overlap.
Slice words from start through start + chunk_size.

lessons.title: Filter with Trustworthy Metadata
lessons.summary: Use access, version, language, and time filters before similarity ranking.

contentBlocks.text: Similarity cannot enforce authorization

Metadata narrows search to documents the requester may access and that fit the task. Tenant ID and permissions should be derived from authenticated server context, never from user-supplied prompt text.
Useful chunk metadata
items: Source and stable document ID
Version and effective date
Section heading and page
Language and content type
Tenant and access-control tags

challenge.instructions: A shared index stores documents for many companies. Choose the safe query design.

choices.text: Apply an authenticated tenant filter inside retrieval before candidates are returned.
Retrieve globally and ask the model not to quote other tenants.
Let the user type any tenant ID into the question.

challenge.explanation: The retrieval layer must prevent unauthorized documents from entering context at all; model instructions are not an access-control boundary.
hints: Unauthorized evidence should never reach the model.
Trust identity from authentication, not prompt text.

lessons.title: Rewrite Follow-Ups for Retrieval
lessons.summary: Create a standalone search query from a short follow-up and known conversation subject.

contentBlocks.text: Search needs the referent, not the pronoun

A follow-up such as "when does it expire?" is meaningful in conversation but poor for search. Query rewriting resolves references using bounded history while preserving the user’s intent; it should not invent new constraints or facts.
Log both original and rewritten queries. Evaluation must catch rewrites that silently change the question.

challenge.instructions: If a subject is known, prefix it to the stripped follow-up; otherwise return the follow-up unchanged.
challenge.explanation: The known subject supplies missing retrieval context while the original question remains intact.
hints: Check that subject exists and is not whitespace.
Return question unchanged without a subject.

modules.title: Generate, Cite, and Evaluate
modules.summary: Assemble evidence into a controlled answer contract and diagnose failures by component.

lessons.title: Assemble Evidence, Not a Document Dump
lessons.summary: Order, deduplicate, label, and budget retrieved passages before generation.

contentBlocks.text: Context assembly is the bridge to generation

Retrieve broadly enough for recall, then rerank, deduplicate overlapping chunks, and include source labels. Order passages by relevance or a task-specific sequence while reserving answer tokens and preserving qualifications.
An evidence packet should expose
items: Stable source ID
Title and section
Exact supporting passage
Version or timestamp
Retrieval or reranking score

challenge.instructions: Explain why five nearly identical overlapping chunks may hurt even when all are relevant.
challenge.explanation: They consume scarce context, overrepresent one source, and can crowd out complementary evidence needed for a complete answer.
hints: Count unique information, not just relevant chunks.
Repeated evidence changes the balance of context.

lessons.title: Make Citations Verifiable
lessons.summary: Attach claims to stable source references rather than trusting model-generated link text.

contentBlocks.text: Citation generation needs source control

Give each retrieved passage an application-assigned source ID and instruct the model to cite only those IDs. After generation, verify every cited ID exists and render the final title and URL from trusted metadata rather than model-written links.
Citation presence is not citation correctness. Evaluate whether the cited passage actually supports the nearby claim.

challenge.instructions: The model returns [S3]. Where should the displayed URL come from?

choices.text: Trusted metadata stored for retrieved source S3.
Any URL the model invents after the answer.
The user’s unverified prompt instructions.

challenge.explanation: Application metadata binds the allowed source ID to an authoritative URL and prevents fabricated links.
hints: The model should select an ID, not author trust metadata.
Verify the ID was in the request context.

lessons.title: Build a Citation-Constrained Prompt
lessons.summary: Render numbered sources and require grounded answers or explicit abstention.

contentBlocks.text: Abstention is part of the output contract

The prompt should permit an "insufficient evidence" response when sources do not support the question. Otherwise the model is pressured to complete an answer from prior knowledge or plausible invention.

Answer only from SOURCES. Cite source IDs after claims.
If the sources are insufficient, say: INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE.

challenge.instructions: Create [id] text lines, then append the question and abstention instruction.
challenge.solution:
def rag_prompt(question, sources):
    lines = []
    for source in sources:
        source_line = f"[{source['id']}] {source['text']}"
        lines.append(source_line)
    evidence = "\n".join(lines)
    rule = "Use only SOURCES and cite IDs. If insufficient, say INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE."
    return f"{rule}\nSOURCES:\n{evidence}\nQUESTION: {question}"

testCases.expected: empty SOURCES section with abstention rule

challenge.explanation: Application-owned IDs make citations checkable, while the explicit insufficient-evidence path prevents forced guessing.
hints: Format each line as [id] text.
Include the rule before evidence and the question after it.

lessons.title: Route RAG Failures to the Right Layer
lessons.summary: Separate corpus, retrieval, reranking, context, and generation defects before choosing a fix.

contentBlocks.text: Inspect the evidence funnel

When an answer fails, first ask whether authoritative content exists in the corpus, then whether it appeared in candidates, survived reranking, fit the final context, and was used faithfully. Changing the generation prompt cannot repair a missing source document.
Failure labels
items: Corpus gap
Parsing or chunking defect
Retrieval miss
Reranking loss
Context truncation
Unsupported generation

challenge.instructions: The correct passage exists and ranks second, but it is removed when only the top one chunk is sent. What should change first?

choices.text: Context-selection policy or final chunk count.
Re-collect the source document.
Train a tokenizer from scratch.

challenge.explanation: Retrieval found the evidence; the loss happens at final context assembly, so that stage is the direct repair target.
hints: Locate the last stage where the passage is present.
Fix the first stage that drops necessary evidence.

lessons.title: Evaluate Retrieval and Answers Separately
lessons.summary: Combine retrieval recall, answer correctness, faithfulness, citation support, and abstention quality.

contentBlocks.text: One end-to-end score hides the repair

A RAG evaluation set should include questions, relevant sources, expected answer facts, and unanswerable cases. Measure candidate recall and ranking separately from answer correctness, evidence faithfulness, citation support, and appropriate abstention.
Include time-sensitive and access-controlled cases so evaluation covers freshness and authorization, not only semantic relevance.

challenge.prompt: Interpret a faithful but incomplete answer
challenge.instructions: Every answer claim is supported, but half the required facts are absent because retrieval missed a document. Which component is the first suspect?

choices.text: Retrieval recall
Citation formatting color
The arithmetic in softmax

challenge.explanation: Faithfulness is good for the supplied evidence, but missing required source facts points to corpus or retrieval recall before generation.
hints: The model did not invent unsupported content.
Ask whether all necessary evidence reached it.

courses.title: LLM Application Architecture
courses.summary: Wrap probabilistic models in typed contracts, gateways, retries, queues, budgets, state, and observable application flows.

modules.title: Typed Contracts and the Model Gateway
modules.summary: Keep business invariants deterministic while centralizing model access and failure handling.

lessons.title: Use a Deterministic Shell
lessons.summary: Place language understanding inside code-enforced authorization, validation, and persistence boundaries.

contentBlocks.text: The model proposes; trusted code disposes

Models are useful for ambiguity, interpretation, and synthesis. Deterministic services should own identity, permissions, prices, quotas, state transitions, and irreversible actions. Treat model output as untrusted input to the next layer.
A safe request path
items: Authenticate and validate input.
Construct bounded context.
Request a typed proposal.
Validate semantics and authorization.
Execute through trusted services.

challenge.instructions: A model suggests refund amounts, but automatic refunds cannot exceed €50. Explain where the cap belongs.
challenge.explanation: The refund service must enforce the cap before any transaction; a prompt may describe the rule but cannot provide the hard guarantee.
hints: Ask which layer controls the actual transfer.
Model output is a proposal, not authorization.

lessons.title: Constrain Output before Parsing
lessons.summary: Use schema-native generation, typed parsing, and domain validation as separate gates.

contentBlocks.text: Valid syntax can still express an invalid action

A schema can require fields and types, greatly reducing malformed output. After parsing, domain checks must still enforce ranges, cross-field relationships, references, and permissions before anything downstream acts.
Preserve raw response, parsed object, validation result, and schema version in traces so failures are diagnosable.

challenge.instructions: The model returns valid JSON with {"discount_percent": 900}. What should the application do?

choices.text: Reject it with domain-range validation before execution.
Apply it because the JSON parsed.
Hide the value in logs and continue.

challenge.explanation: Schema syntax does not establish business validity; a 900% discount violates a range invariant and must be rejected.
hints: Parsing answers "is it shaped correctly?" only.
A business rule answers "is this allowed?"

lessons.title: Validate a Model Proposal
lessons.summary: Convert typed output into either an accepted domain object or explicit validation errors.

contentBlocks.text: Make rejected states observable
A validator should collect precise reasons rather than returning a vague false. Error codes support retries, monitoring, and human review while keeping policy logic outside prompt text.

challenge.instructions: Return error codes when amount is negative, exceeds the limit, or reason is blank.
challenge.starterCode:
def validate_refund(proposal, limit):
    errors = []
    amount = proposal["amount"]
    if amount < 0:
        errors.append("negative_amount")
    ____
    ____
    return errors
challenge.explanation: Independent checks preserve every violated invariant, producing useful feedback without trusting the model to self-police.
hints: Compare amount > limit.
Get reason with an empty fallback and strip whitespace.

lessons.title: Centralize Providers behind a Gateway
lessons.summary: Create one internal interface for provider calls, policy, telemetry, and controlled fallback.

contentBlocks.text: Applications should depend on capabilities, not vendor payloads

A model gateway translates an internal request contract into provider-specific APIs. It centralizes authentication, model allowlists, timeouts, retries, rate limits, logging, redaction, cost attribution, and feature compatibility.
Avoid a lowest-common-denominator abstraction: expose capabilities such as structured output, tools, vision, and streaming explicitly and reject unsupported combinations.

challenge.instructions: The primary model times out during a schema-extraction request. Choose a safe fallback policy.

choices.text: Fallback only to an approved model supporting the same schema contract, then revalidate output.
Use any available text model and skip validation.
Retry forever without a deadline.

challenge.explanation: Fallback must preserve required capabilities and output guarantees; validation remains necessary regardless of provider.
hints: Feature compatibility is part of the contract.
Fallback changes the model, not the business rules.

lessons.title: Retry Only Transient Failures
lessons.summary: Classify retryable statuses and calculate bounded exponential backoff with jitter-ready structure.

contentBlocks.text: Retries consume time, money, and capacity

Rate limits, timeouts, and temporary server failures may recover. Invalid requests, failed authorization, and impossible schema constraints usually will not. Bound attempts by a request deadline and make consequential operations idempotent before retrying.

delay = min(base_delay * (2 ** attempt), max_delay)
# Add small random jitter in production.

challenge.instructions: Retry 429 and 5xx statuses, and return capped exponential delay; otherwise return None.
challenge.solution:
def retry_delay(status, attempt, base=0.5, maximum=8.0):
    retryable = status == 429 or status >= 500
    if not retryable:
        return None
    exponential_delay = base * (2 ** attempt)
    delay = min(exponential_delay, maximum)
    return delay
challenge.explanation: Only transient status classes receive backoff, and the maximum prevents waits from growing without bound.
hints: Compute base * 2 raised to attempt.
Use min with maximum and return the result.

modules.title: Runtime Flow, State, and Budgets
modules.summary: Choose synchronous, streamed, or queued execution and protect the system under load.

lessons.title: Synchronous, Streaming, and Asynchronous Work
lessons.summary: Match the user experience and failure model to the duration and interactivity of a task.

contentBlocks.text: Execution mode is a product decision

A short classification can complete synchronously. Streaming improves perceived latency for an answer consumed as it arrives. Long document jobs should enter a durable queue with status, cancellation, retries, and stored results so they survive client disconnects.
Streaming changes delivery, not correctness. Validate the completed structured result before executing downstream actions.

challenge.instructions: A report analyzes 500 documents and may take ten minutes. Explain the appropriate pattern.
challenge.explanation: Submit a durable asynchronous job, return a job ID, expose progress and cancellation, checkpoint work, and notify or let the client poll for the stored result.
hints: The client connection may not stay open ten minutes.
The work should survive process and network interruptions.

lessons.title: Protect Capacity with Backpressure
lessons.summary: Limit in-flight work and queue growth before overload becomes cascading failure.

contentBlocks.text: Unlimited queues convert overload into delayed failure

Concurrency limits bound expensive model calls. Bounded queues reject, defer, or degrade excess traffic instead of consuming all memory and waiting beyond useful deadlines. Per-tenant quotas prevent one customer from exhausting shared capacity.
Overload controls
items: Global and per-tenant concurrency
Bounded queue depth
Request deadlines
Priority classes
Cheaper degradation paths
Retry-after signals

challenge.instructions: All workers are busy and queued jobs already exceed their useful deadline. What is the safest behavior?

choices.text: Reject or defer new work with a clear retry signal rather than growing the queue.
Accept unlimited work until the process crashes.
Hide queue delay from clients.

challenge.explanation: Backpressure preserves system recovery and gives callers actionable information instead of accepting work that cannot succeed on time.
hints: A queued request can become useless before execution.
Bound memory and time, not only worker count.

lessons.title: Route Requests within a Budget
lessons.summary: Select the least costly approved model that satisfies capability and token requirements.

contentBlocks.text: Model choice can be a policy function

A router should filter candidates by required capabilities and context size before comparing price or latency. Recording the decision reason makes cost changes explainable and supports offline replay against production traffic.

eligible = [m for m in models if required <= set(m["capabilities"]) and tokens <= m["context"]]
return min(eligible, key=lambda m: m["cost"])

challenge.instructions: Filter by required capability and sufficient context, then return the lowest-cost model name or None.
challenge.explanation: Capability and context are hard constraints; cost optimizes only among candidates that can actually perform the task.
hints: Require supports and fits together.
Use min with model cost as the key.

lessons.title: Separate Conversation and Business State
lessons.summary: Keep chat history, workflow state, and system-of-record data under different consistency rules.

contentBlocks.text: A transcript is not a database transaction

Conversation state supports linguistic continuity and can be summarized or pruned. Business state—orders, approvals, balances—must live in authoritative services with versioning and concurrency control. The model receives a snapshot and requests actions through validated commands.
Use idempotency keys for retried actions and optimistic version checks when a proposal depends on state that may have changed.

challenge.instructions: The model saw five items in stock, but inventory may change before purchase. Choose the correct boundary.

choices.text: The inventory service rechecks stock and state version when executing the requested purchase.
The model’s earlier context becomes the permanent source of truth.
Skip concurrency checks because the assistant sounded confident.

challenge.explanation: Authoritative state must be checked at execution time; model context is a potentially stale snapshot.
hints: State can change after prompt construction.
Execution belongs to the service that owns inventory.

lessons.title: Trace a Production Request End to End
lessons.summary: Place authentication, retrieval, model calls, validation, execution, and telemetry in a defensible order.

contentBlocks.text: Reliability emerges from the whole path

A production request crosses trust and failure boundaries. Authenticate first, establish a deadline and trace, load authorized context, call the gateway, parse and validate output, execute idempotently if allowed, and record outcome metrics without leaking sensitive content.
Observability spans every boundary
items: Request and trace IDs
Prompt and schema versions
Retrieval source IDs
Model, latency, tokens, and cost
Validation and action outcomes
User-visible error category

courses.title: Agents & Tool-Using Systems
courses.summary: Engineer bounded agents that choose tools, preserve state, recover from failure, and respect real authorization boundaries.

modules.title: Agent Control Loops
modules.summary: Turn open-ended reasoning into a bounded, inspectable state machine.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Bounded Agent
lessons.summary: Separate model reasoning from the deterministic loop that owns limits and state.

contentBlocks.text: Anatomy of a Bounded Agent

An agent is a controller around a model: it assembles context, asks for a proposed action, validates that action, executes an allowed tool, records the observation, and repeats. Reliability comes from the controller rather than hoping the model stops at the right time.
Production reasoning
items: Represent every turn as an explicit state transition.
Cap steps, elapsed time, tokens, and tool spend.
Terminate on success, policy refusal, or exhausted budget.

contentBlocks.text: The model may propose actions, but deterministic code decides whether an action may run.

challenge.prompt: Apply the principle: Anatomy of a Bounded Agent
challenge.instructions: Choose the answer that best matches the production principle in this lesson.

choices.text: A deterministic controller validates actions and enforces several budgets.
A longer system prompt alone makes the loop bounded.
The model should execute tools directly to reduce latency.

challenge.explanation: The model may propose actions, but deterministic code decides whether an action may run.
hints: Represent every turn as an explicit state transition.
Cap steps, elapsed time, tokens, and tool spend.

lessons.title: Tool Schemas as Contracts
lessons.summary: Design schemas that make invalid actions difficult to express.

contentBlocks.text: Tool Schemas as Contracts

A tool schema is an API contract presented to a probabilistic caller. Narrow enums, required fields, unambiguous units, and explicit error shapes reduce malformed calls and make validation failures teachable to the model.
Production reasoning
items: Use domain types instead of free-form strings.
Describe side effects and permission requirements.
Return stable machine-readable error codes.

contentBlocks.text: A permissive schema shifts ambiguity into runtime, where it becomes expensive and dangerous.

challenge.prompt: Apply the principle: Tool Schemas as Contracts
challenge.instructions: Choose the answer that best matches the production principle in this lesson.

choices.text: Define currency as an enum and amount as a positive integer of minor units.
Accept one free-form command string and parse it inside the tool.
Let the model infer units from prior messages.

challenge.explanation: A permissive schema shifts ambiguity into runtime, where it becomes expensive and dangerous.
hints: Use domain types instead of free-form strings.
Describe side effects and permission requirements.

lessons.title: Implement a Step-Bounded Loop
lessons.summary: Code a controller that cannot recurse forever.

contentBlocks.text: Implement a Step-Bounded Loop

A robust loop checks termination before every model call, treats tool errors as observations instead of crashes, and returns a typed terminal reason. This makes runaway behavior testable and lets callers distinguish success from budget exhaustion.
Production reasoning
items: Increment the counter in one deterministic location.
Validate proposed actions before dispatch.
Persist the final reason for evaluation and debugging.

challenge.explanation: The loop owns the budget and emits explicit terminal states, so the model cannot silently exceed limits.
hints: Increment the counter in one deterministic location.
Validate proposed actions before dispatch.
The loop owns the budget and emits explicit terminal states, so the model cannot silently exceed limits.

lessons.title: State, Memory, and Event Logs
lessons.summary: Choose state stores by lifetime and correctness needs.

contentBlocks.text: State, Memory, and Event Logs

Working state supports the current task; episodic memory records prior events; semantic memory stores extracted facts. Mixing them into one unbounded transcript raises cost, leaks stale assumptions, and makes deletion or correction nearly impossible.
Production reasoning
items: Keep an append-only event log for auditability.
Build compact working state from relevant events.
Attach provenance and expiry to remembered facts.

contentBlocks.text: Memory is a data product with retention, correction, and access-control requirements—not simply a bigger prompt.

challenge.instructions: Choose the architecture that best preserves the stated invariants under realistic failure.

choices.text: Use an event log plus derived, scoped memory views with provenance.
Append every conversation to every new prompt.
Store model-written summaries without source links or expiry.

challenge.explanation: Memory is a data product with retention, correction, and access-control requirements—not simply a bigger prompt.
hints: Keep an append-only event log for auditability.
Build compact working state from relevant events.

lessons.title: Normalize Tool Results
lessons.summary: Build one result envelope for success, retry, and refusal.

contentBlocks.text: Normalize Tool Results

Agents reason more reliably when every tool returns the same outer shape. A normalized envelope separates a stable status code from user-safe detail, retry guidance, and structured data, so the controller can branch without parsing prose.
Production reasoning
items: Distinguish retryable failures from permanent rejections.
Exclude secrets and raw stack traces from observations.
Preserve a correlation ID across execution.

challenge.instructions: Edit the Python implementation so it satisfies the contract and all structural checks. Preserve explicit failure handling.
challenge.explanation: A stable envelope gives the loop deterministic branching while providing the model a safe observation.
hints: Distinguish retryable failures from permanent rejections.
Exclude secrets and raw stack traces from observations.
A stable envelope gives the loop deterministic branching while providing the model a safe observation.

modules.title: Reliable Agent Orchestration
modules.summary: Add planning, permissions, idempotency, collaboration, and recovery.

lessons.title: Planning Without Pretending
lessons.summary: Use plans as revisable hypotheses, not guaranteed scripts.

contentBlocks.text: Planning Without Pretending

Plans expose dependencies and missing information, but tools return surprises. Reliable agents interleave short planning horizons with observations and re-planning instead of committing to a long chain built on unverified assumptions.
Production reasoning
items: Plan irreversible steps more carefully than reads.
Record assumptions observations can invalidate.
Re-plan after material changes, not every token.

contentBlocks.text: Planning is valuable when it improves control and observability; hidden reasoning is not an operational artifact.

challenge.prompt: Apply the principle: Planning Without Pretending
challenge.instructions: Choose the answer that best matches the production principle in this lesson.

choices.text: Store an explicit task graph of actions, dependencies, assumptions, and statuses.
Ask for a private reasoning trace and execute it verbatim.
Skip planning because all tools can be retried.

challenge.explanation: Planning is valuable when it improves control and observability; hidden reasoning is not an operational artifact.
hints: Plan irreversible steps more carefully than reads.
Record assumptions observations can invalidate.

lessons.title: Capability-Based Permissions
lessons.summary: Grant the smallest authority needed for one task.

contentBlocks.text: Capability-Based Permissions

Authentication identifies the caller; authorization determines allowed actions; capability tokens can further scope a call to a resource, operation, amount, and expiry. The agent should never infer authority from conversational intent.
Production reasoning
items: Separate read, draft, approve, and execute capabilities.
Require human approval for high-impact transitions.
Re-check authorization inside the tool service.

contentBlocks.text: A prompt cannot grant permission; the service performing the side effect must verify a scoped capability.

challenge.instructions: Choose the answer that best matches the production principle in this lesson.

choices.text: Issue a short-lived token limited to refund order 481 by at most €50.
Give the agent a permanent administrator token in its prompt.
Treat a user's request as proof of authorization.

challenge.explanation: A prompt cannot grant permission; the service performing the side effect must verify a scoped capability.
hints: Separate read, draft, approve, and execute capabilities.
Require human approval for high-impact transitions.

lessons.title: Make Tool Execution Idempotent
lessons.summary: Prevent retries from duplicating side effects.

contentBlocks.text: Make Tool Execution Idempotent
Networks fail after a server commits but before the agent sees the response. An idempotency key lets the service return the original result instead of charging, emailing, or provisioning twice.
Production reasoning
items: Derive the key from a stable logical operation ID.
Store the committed result alongside the key.
Reject key reuse with different arguments.

challenge.explanation: Binding the key to an argument fingerprint prevents duplicate execution and accidental key reuse.
hints: Derive the key from a stable logical operation ID.
Store the committed result alongside the key.
Binding the key to an argument fingerprint prevents duplicate execution and accidental key reuse.

lessons.title: Multi-Agent Topologies
lessons.summary: Choose specialization only when boundaries are observable.

contentBlocks.text: Multi-Agent Topologies

Multiple agents can isolate contexts and permissions, but every handoff adds latency, cost, and another place to lose intent. Coordinator-worker designs are justified when tasks have distinct tools, access policies, or parallelizable outputs.
Production reasoning
items: Define typed handoff payloads and completion criteria.
Give each worker only the tools it needs.
Trace the parent task across delegated spans.

contentBlocks.text: More agents do not automatically mean more intelligence; topology should follow isolation, parallelism, or expertise needs.

challenge.instructions: Choose the architecture that best preserves the stated invariants under realistic failure.

choices.text: Use a coordinator with typed tasks and scoped specialist workers.

Create one agent per prompt paragraph regardless of dependencies.

challenge.explanation: More agents do not automatically mean more intelligence; topology should follow isolation, parallelism, or expertise needs.
hints: Define typed handoff payloads and completion criteria.
Give each worker only the tools it needs.

lessons.title: Recovery Budgets and Escalation
lessons.summary: Implement retries that stop before they become incidents.

contentBlocks.text: Recovery Budgets and Escalation

Retry policy combines attempt count, elapsed time, error class, and side-effect safety. Backoff reduces synchronized load, while escalation preserves the task state an operator needs to continue safely.
Production reasoning
items: Retry only errors classified as transient.
Use jitter to avoid a thundering herd.
Escalate with evidence and remaining choices.

courses.title: Evaluation Engineering
courses.summary: Build evaluation systems that detect quality regressions, quantify uncertainty, and connect offline evidence to production outcomes.

modules.title: Evaluation Foundations
modules.summary: Define behavior, datasets, metrics, and uncertainty before comparing systems.

lessons.title: The Evaluation Contract
lessons.summary: Translate a product promise into observable pass and fail criteria.

contentBlocks.text: The Evaluation Contract

An evaluation contract names the population, task, acceptable behavior, forbidden behavior, and release decision the result will inform. Without it, a score can improve while the product becomes worse for important users.
Production reasoning
items: Specify the unit: turn, conversation, task, or outcome.
Separate hard constraints from graded preferences.
Name the release decision and minimum evidence.

contentBlocks.text: A metric is useful only when its boundary matches the product claim.

challenge.prompt: Apply the principle: The Evaluation Contract
challenge.instructions: Choose the production-safe answer.

choices.text: Define success, safety constraints, target slices, and release thresholds first.
Choose a popular benchmark without mapping it to users.
Report one average and let stakeholders interpret it.

challenge.explanation: A metric is useful only when its boundary matches the product claim.
hints: Specify the unit: turn, conversation, task, or outcome.
Separate hard constraints from graded preferences.

lessons.title: Representative Evaluation Sets
lessons.summary: Sample cases to expose the distribution you actually serve.

contentBlocks.text: Representative Evaluation Sets

A useful set combines common traffic, high-impact rare cases, known failures, adversarial probes, and time-based holdouts. Random convenience samples often hide the tails that determine operational risk.
Production reasoning
items: Attach slice labels and provenance to every case.
Deduplicate near copies across train and test.
Version cases and record why each was added.

contentBlocks.text: The goal is coverage of consequential behavior, not merely a large row count.

challenge.prompt: Apply the principle: Representative Evaluation Sets
challenge.instructions: Choose the production-safe answer.

choices.text: Stratify by traffic, impact, language, and failure history; reserve a temporal holdout.
Copy training examples into the test set.
Use only easy cases so changes are quick to verify.

challenge.explanation: The goal is coverage of consequential behavior, not merely a large row count.
hints: Attach slice labels and provenance to every case.
Deduplicate near copies across train and test.

lessons.title: Implement Precision, Recall, and F1
lessons.summary: Compute metrics from explicit confusion counts.

contentBlocks.text: Implement Precision, Recall, and F1

Accuracy can look excellent when failures are rare. Precision asks whether positive predictions are trustworthy; recall asks whether actual positives are found; F1 balances them but still needs slice-level interpretation.
Production reasoning
items: Guard against zero denominators.
Return component metrics, not only F1.
Keep the classification threshold outside this function.

Return component metrics, not only F1.

lessons.title: Designing Model-Judge Evaluations
lessons.summary: Use model graders with rubrics, calibration, and human audits.

contentBlocks.text: Designing Model-Judge Evaluations

A model judge scales evaluation of open-ended outputs but inherits biases, prompt sensitivity, and correlated failures. Strong designs use a concrete rubric, blinded answer order, evidence when appropriate, and human calibration samples.
Production reasoning
items: Measure agreement with expert labels by slice.
Randomize candidate order to detect position bias.
Retain judge rationale for audit, not as truth.

contentBlocks.text: A judge is another measurement instrument; calibrate it before trusting its score.

challenge.instructions: Choose the architecture that preserves the invariants under realistic failure.

choices.text: Run rubric-based blinded judging and send disagreements to human review.
Ask the candidate model to grade its own unblinded answer.
Use one vague question such as 'Is this good?' for every task.

challenge.explanation: A judge is another measurement instrument; calibrate it before trusting its score.
hints: Measure agreement with expert labels by slice.
Randomize candidate order to detect position bias.

lessons.title: Bootstrap a Confidence Interval
lessons.summary: Quantify uncertainty without assuming a convenient score distribution.

contentBlocks.text: Bootstrap a Confidence Interval

Bootstrapping repeatedly resamples evaluation cases with replacement and recomputes the statistic. A percentile interval shows how much a mean could move due to finite sampling; paired comparisons reuse sampled indices.
Production reasoning
items: Seed randomness for reproducible tests.
Resample cases, not token observations.
For comparisons, bootstrap paired score differences.

modules.title: Production Evaluation
modules.summary: Gate releases, run online experiments, and turn failures into durable cases.

lessons.title: Slices, Tails, and Adversarial Cases
lessons.summary: Find failures hidden by aggregate averages.

contentBlocks.text: Slices, Tails, and Adversarial Cases

A system can meet its average target while failing a language, device, intent, or safety-sensitive subgroup. Slice evaluation exposes disparity; adversarial cases probe whether the design fails predictably when inputs exploit assumptions.
Production reasoning
items: Pre-register critical slices before seeing results.
Require sample sizes or uncertainty bounds.
Track worst-slice performance beside the global score.

contentBlocks.text: Release decisions should consider users most harmed by error, not only users most common.

challenge.prompt: Apply the principle: Slices, Tails, and Adversarial Cases
challenge.instructions: Choose the production-safe answer.

choices.text: Report global, critical-slice, and worst-slice metrics with uncertainty.
Merge every case into one average.
Remove adversarial cases because they are atypical.

challenge.explanation: Release decisions should consider users most harmed by error, not only users most common.
hints: Pre-register critical slices before seeing results.
Require sample sizes or uncertainty bounds.

lessons.title: Regression Gates That Match Risk
lessons.summary: Use thresholds, deltas, and hard constraints to make release decisions.

contentBlocks.text: Regression Gates That Match Risk

A regression gate should block meaningful harm without freezing development over noise. Combine non-negotiable safety checks, minimum absolute quality, allowed degradation from baseline, and uncertainty-aware review for borderline results.
Production reasoning
items: Pin baseline, dataset, and evaluator versions.
Treat critical safety failures as case-level blockers.
Route ambiguous changes to manual review.

contentBlocks.text: A gate is a policy decision backed by measurement, not a single magic score.

challenge.prompt: Apply the principle: Regression Gates That Match Risk
challenge.instructions: Choose the production-safe answer.

choices.text: Block safety violations, require slice minima, and review uncertain deltas.
Release whenever the global average exceeds 50%.
Change the test set after seeing which cases fail.

challenge.explanation: A gate is a policy decision backed by measurement, not a single magic score.
hints: Pin baseline, dataset, and evaluator versions.
Treat critical safety failures as case-level blockers.

lessons.title: Build a Pairwise Preference Evaluator
lessons.summary: Compare candidates while controlling answer-order bias.

contentBlocks.text: Build a Pairwise Preference Evaluator

Pairwise evaluation is easier than assigning absolute scores, but judges may favor the first or longer answer. Evaluate both orderings, map labels back to stable IDs, and treat inconsistent judgments as review items.
Production reasoning
items: Swap candidate order and map results back.
Represent tie and inconsistency explicitly.
Do not infer a winner when judge calls fail.

Mapping the swapped vote exposes position-sensitive disagreements rather than hiding them.

lessons.title: Online Experiments for AI Features
lessons.summary: Connect behavioral quality to real user outcomes safely.

contentBlocks.text: Online Experiments for AI Features

Offline evaluations are reproducible but incomplete; online experiments capture adoption, corrections, latency, and downstream impact. Start with guardrails and a small ramp, randomize at a contamination-safe unit, and predefine stopping conditions.
Production reasoning
items: Randomize by user when conversation context carries over.
Log assignment before model execution.
Monitor harm, latency, and cost during the ramp.

contentBlocks.text: An experiment should stop automatically before a promising feature causes unacceptable harm.

challenge.instructions: Choose the architecture that preserves the invariants under realistic failure.

choices.text: Randomize by user, ramp gradually, and auto-stop on safety or latency guardrails.
Assign each message independently within one conversation.
Expose everyone immediately to reach significance faster.

challenge.explanation: An experiment should stop automatically before a promising feature causes unacceptable harm.
hints: Randomize by user when conversation context carries over.
Log assignment before model execution.

lessons.title: Turn Failures Into Triage Buckets
lessons.summary: Cluster failures by actionable root cause instead of vague quality labels.

contentBlocks.text: Turn Failures Into Triage Buckets

Evaluation becomes an engineering loop when each failure maps to a layer that can change: data, retrieval, prompt, model capability, tool, policy, or product interaction. A deterministic first pass creates ownership.
Production reasoning
items: Preserve raw evidence and evaluator version.
Allow an unknown bucket rather than forcing certainty.
Count severity and recurrence separately.

courses.title: Safety, Security & Guardrails
courses.summary: Threat-model AI applications, constrain privileges, resist injection, and operate layered safety controls.

modules.title: Threats and Enforcement Boundaries
modules.summary: Identify adversaries and enforce policy outside probabilistic components.

lessons.title: Threat-Model the Whole AI System
lessons.summary: Map assets, trust boundaries, attackers, and abuse paths before choosing controls.

contentBlocks.text: Threat-Model the Whole AI System

AI threats cross ordinary application layers: untrusted text enters through users, retrieved documents, tools, or model outputs. A threat model follows data and authority across those boundaries and asks what an attacker gains when any probabilistic assumption fails.
Production reasoning
items: Inventory secrets, private data, money movement, and publishing rights.
Mark every transition from untrusted to privileged context.
Model insider misuse and accidental failure too.

contentBlocks.text: The model is neither the only attack surface nor a security boundary; analyze the complete data-and-tool path.

challenge.prompt: Apply the principle: Threat-Model the Whole AI System
challenge.instructions: Choose the production-safe answer.

choices.text: Draw assets, actors, trust boundaries, entry points, and mitigations end to end.
List only undesirable words the model might output.
Assume retrieved internal documents are automatically trusted.

challenge.explanation: The model is neither the only attack surface nor a security boundary; analyze the complete data-and-tool path.
hints: Inventory secrets, private data, money movement, and publishing rights.
Mark every transition from untrusted to privileged context.

lessons.title: Prompt Injection Is Untrusted Data
lessons.summary: Treat instructions inside content as data unless a trusted controller grants authority.

contentBlocks.text: Prompt Injection Is Untrusted Data

Prompt injection exploits the model's difficulty separating commands from quoted or retrieved content. Delimiters help, but robust defense minimizes tool privilege, labels provenance, validates actions, and keeps policy enforcement deterministic.
Production reasoning
items: Classify each context source by trust and authority.
Never let retrieved text redefine permissions.
Confirm consequential or surprising actions.

contentBlocks.text: No prompt can make arbitrary hostile text safe; containment limits what successful injection can do.

challenge.prompt: Apply the principle: Prompt Injection Is Untrusted Data
challenge.instructions: Choose the production-safe answer.

choices.text: Pass documents as untrusted evidence and validate proposed tool calls against policy.
Tell the model once to ignore malicious instructions.
Concatenate web pages into the system prompt so they inherit authority.

challenge.explanation: No prompt can make arbitrary hostile text safe; containment limits what successful injection can do.
hints: Classify each context source by trust and authority.
Never let retrieved text redefine permissions.

lessons.title: Validate Tool Arguments Against Policy
lessons.summary: Reject syntactically valid calls that exceed business or permission rules.

contentBlocks.text: Validate Tool Arguments Against Policy
JSON schema validates shape, while policy validation checks meaning: ownership, limits, destinations, and task scope. Tool services enforce both because model-proposed arguments remain untrusted.
Production reasoning
items: Fail closed when identity or scope is missing.
Return stable rejection codes without leaking policy detail.
Audit actor, capability, resource, and decision.

lessons.title: Layered Policy Enforcement
lessons.summary: Place controls before, during, and after model execution.

contentBlocks.text: Layered Policy Enforcement

Input checks can reject abuse, the model follows behavioral guidance, tool gateways enforce capabilities, and output validators catch prohibited disclosure. Layering matters because each individual detector has false positives and negatives.
Production reasoning
items: Use deterministic controls for hard invariants.
Log which layer made each allow, block, or escalate decision.
Design a safe fallback when a detector is unavailable.

contentBlocks.text: Defense in depth means independent controls with explicit ownership, not several prompts that fail together.

challenge.instructions: Choose the architecture that preserves invariants under realistic failure.

choices.text: Use input risk checks, scoped tools, output validation, and escalation.
Put every rule into one system prompt and remove service checks.
Run only an output keyword filter after privileged actions complete.

challenge.explanation: Defense in depth means independent controls with explicit ownership, not several prompts that fail together.
hints: Use deterministic controls for hard invariants.
Log which layer made each allow, block, or escalate decision.

lessons.title: Build an Output Contract Validator
lessons.summary: Validate citations and sensitive fields before displaying model output.

contentBlocks.text: Build an Output Contract Validator

Output validation parses a typed response, verifies required evidence, scans for disallowed data classes, and chooses a fail-safe action. It distinguishes repairable formatting from semantic violations that must not be retried into disclosure.
Production reasoning
items: Parse structure before rendering any field.
Verify cited IDs against retrieved evidence.
Redact or block using a documented severity policy.

modules.title: Secure AI Operations
modules.summary: Protect capabilities, control abuse, respond to incidents, and continuously red-team.

lessons.title: Secrets, Identity, and Capabilities
lessons.summary: Keep credentials out of prompts and bind every action to verifiable identity.

contentBlocks.text: Secrets, Identity, and Capabilities

Prompts, traces, and transcripts are copied into debugging systems, making them unsafe secret stores. Credentials belong in a secrets manager; a tool gateway exchanges workload identity for short-lived scoped capabilities only when an authorized action is ready.
Production reasoning
items: Use workload identity instead of shared static keys.
Mint credentials with narrow audience, scope, and expiry.
Redact credential-like values before tracing.

contentBlocks.text: The agent can reference a capability handle, but raw credentials should never enter model context.

challenge.instructions: Choose the production-safe answer.

choices.text: Resolve a short-lived scoped credential inside the tool service after authorization.
Embed a production token in the system prompt.
Give every agent the same permanent service key.

challenge.explanation: The agent can reference a capability handle, but raw credentials should never enter model context.
hints: Use workload identity instead of shared static keys.
Mint credentials with narrow audience, scope, and expiry.

lessons.title: AI Supply-Chain Security
lessons.summary: Verify models, datasets, packages, and prompt assets as deployable artifacts.

contentBlocks.text: AI Supply-Chain Security

A compromised model file, tokenizer, dependency, evaluation dataset, or prompt template can bypass source review. Pin versions and digests, scan serialized artifacts, record provenance, and promote only reproducible checked artifacts.
Production reasoning
items: Prefer safe tensor formats over arbitrary deserialization.
Generate a software and model bill of materials.
Separate build-time network access from runtime serving.

contentBlocks.text: AI supply chains include data and model artifacts, not just conventional packages.

challenge.instructions: Choose the production-safe answer.

Download the latest model at every process start.
Trust a file because its repository is popular.

challenge.explanation: AI supply chains include data and model artifacts, not just conventional packages.
hints: Prefer safe tensor formats over arbitrary deserialization.
Generate a software and model bill of materials.

lessons.title: Compute a Risk-Aware Rate Limit
lessons.summary: Allocate stricter budgets when identity, action, or anomaly risk rises.

contentBlocks.text: Compute a Risk-Aware Rate Limit

Flat request limits ignore that read-only summaries and privileged bulk actions have different blast radii. A risk-aware limiter combines identity reputation, impact, anomalies, and cost while preserving a hard ceiling.
Production reasoning
items: Keep the final deny decision deterministic.
Use concurrency-safe monotonic windows.
Return retry timing without exposing risk features.

lessons.title: Incident Response for AI Systems
lessons.summary: Preserve evidence and revoke authority before debating model behavior.

contentBlocks.text: Incident Response for AI Systems

An AI incident may involve leaked data, abusive automation, corrupted retrieval, or regression. Response begins by limiting blast radius: disable affected capabilities, freeze versions, preserve restricted traces, and switch to a known safe mode.
Production reasoning
items: Maintain kill switches per tool and tenant.
Record model, prompt, index, policy, and evaluator versions.
Separate communication facts from speculative root cause.

contentBlocks.text: Fast rollback requires every behavior-affecting artifact to be versioned and independently deployable.

Delete traces to reduce further disclosure risk.

Red teaming becomes durable when attacks encode goals, entry channels, expected controls, and severity. The harness distinguishes model refusal from end-to-end containment: an injection can succeed linguistically while the tool gateway still prevents harm.

Assert textual behavior and side-effect absence.

lessons.title: Modalities, Encoders, and Shared Meaning
lessons.summary: Understand how different signals become model-consumable representations.

contentBlocks.text: Modalities, Encoders, and Shared Meaning

Text arrives as tokens, images as spatial patches, and audio as time-frequency frames. A multimodal system preserves each modality's distinctions while aligning representations enough for cross-modal reasoning.
Production reasoning
items: Track spatial coordinates for visual grounding.
Track timestamps for audio and video claims.
Preserve the original asset and transformations.

contentBlocks.text: Shared embeddings enable comparison but do not erase modality-specific uncertainty or provenance.

lessons.title: Image Preprocessing Without Evidence Loss
lessons.summary: Transform images deterministically and retain the mapping back to originals.

contentBlocks.text: Image Preprocessing Without Evidence Loss

Resizing, cropping, rotation, color conversion, and compression change what a model can see. Production pipelines log transforms, use quality checks, and map predictions back to original coordinates before displaying them or triggering actions.
Production reasoning
items: Respect orientation metadata before resizing.
Letterbox when distortion would alter geometry.
Reject images below a task-specific detail threshold.

Higher resolution reveals small objects but consumes more visual tokens and compute. A scheduler reserves text capacity, estimates tile value, and allocates the remainder by task priority instead of always sending maximum resolution.

lessons.title: Early, Late, and Tool-Based Fusion
lessons.summary: Select where modalities interact based on task and evidence needs.

contentBlocks.text: Early, Late, and Tool-Based Fusion

Early fusion lets one model jointly attend; late fusion combines independent outputs; tool-based fusion calls specialists. Joint reasoning favors early fusion, while modular auditability and independent scaling often favor later fusion.
Production reasoning
items: Measure cross-modal dependency before adding coupling.
Keep per-modality confidence when combining outputs.
Define what happens when modalities disagree.

A detector may operate on a letterboxed image while the product displays the original. Undo padding and scale correctly so overlays and downstream crops target the evidence users actually see.

lessons.title: Streaming Audio Is a Timeline
lessons.summary: Treat speech recognition as revisable time-indexed evidence.

contentBlocks.text: Streaming Audio Is a Timeline

Streaming transcription emits partial hypotheses that change as audio arrives. Applications distinguish interim from final segments, retain timestamps and speaker labels, and avoid irreversible actions from unstable text.
Production reasoning
items: Use voice activity detection to bound utterances.
Attach timestamps, confidence, and revision IDs.
Wait for finalization before consequential tools.

lessons.title: OCR as Evidence, Not Truth
lessons.summary: Combine extraction confidence, layout, and source crops.

contentBlocks.text: OCR as Evidence, Not Truth

OCR failures vary across small fonts, tables, handwriting, glare, and scripts. Store tokens with coordinates and confidence, preserve source crops, and route low-confidence critical fields to another extractor or human.
Production reasoning
items: Validate dates, totals, and identifiers with domain rules.
Use layout relationships, not reading order alone.
Measure field accuracy by document type.

contentBlocks.text: Chunk Timestamped Transcripts

Retrieval over recordings works better when chunks follow semantic pauses and retain timestamps. Fixed windows can split a decision from its owner; group adjacent utterances within a duration cap and add overlap.

items: Never reorder utterances during normalization.
Retain speaker labels in text and metadata.
Use overlap IDs so repeated evidence can deduplicate.

lessons.title: Realtime Voice Architecture
lessons.summary: Balance interruption handling, latency, and turn consistency.

contentBlocks.text: Realtime Voice Architecture

A voice system pipelines capture, recognition, generation, synthesis, and playback. Barge-in must cancel generation and audio atomically, while one turn ID prevents late packets from speaking an obsolete response.
Production reasoning
items: Propagate cancellation from playback to generation.
Use sequence numbers to reject stale outputs.
Budget first-audio and completion latency separately.

Confidence values from different models are not automatically comparable. Calibrate each modality, apply task-specific reliability weights, and surface disagreement instead of averaging it away.

Downweight missing or low-quality modalities.
Return disagreement for review policies.

courses.title: Fine-Tuning & Adaptation
courses.summary: Choose and operate adaptation strategies from prompting and retrieval through parameter-efficient and full fine-tuning.

modules.title: Adaptation Strategy and Data
modules.summary: Select the lightest effective method and build trustworthy training examples.

lessons.title: The Adaptation Ladder
lessons.summary: Escalate from prompts to retrieval to fine-tuning only when evidence supports it.

contentBlocks.text: The Adaptation Ladder

Prompting changes instructions, retrieval supplies changing knowledge, fine-tuning changes learned behavior, and full training changes broad capacity at highest cost. Diagnose knowledge, behavior, context, or capability failures before choosing a rung.
Production reasoning
items: Use retrieval for private or changing facts.
Use supervised tuning for repeated behavior patterns.
Require measured gain before accepting complexity.

contentBlocks.text: Fine-tuning is not a database update; weights are hard to inspect, correct, or selectively forget.

lessons.title: Curating High-Signal Training Data
lessons.summary: Prefer correct, diverse, traceable examples over sheer volume.

contentBlocks.text: Curating High-Signal Training Data

Training data encodes behavior the model will imitate. Deduplicate near copies, resolve conflicting labels, preserve consent and provenance, balance important slices, and isolate evaluation examples from training decisions.
Production reasoning
items: Write a labeling guide with boundary examples.
Track annotator disagreement rather than erasing it.
Audit safety-sensitive slices separately.

contentBlocks.text: Ten thousand inconsistent examples can teach weaker behavior than one thousand adjudicated examples.

lessons.summary: Validate roles and assistant targets for supervised learning.

contentBlocks.text: Format Chat Training Examples

Chat fine-tuning predicts assistant output conditioned on system and user turns. Formatting errors can train the model to imitate users or leak metadata; validation enforces role order, content, and an assistant target.
Production reasoning
items: Apply the exact serving template in preprocessing.
Reject unknown roles instead of remapping them.
Record truncation so lost targets are visible.

lessons.title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Design
lessons.summary: Use adapters when specialization does not justify copying every weight.

contentBlocks.text: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Design

LoRA learns low-rank updates while the base stays frozen. It reduces memory and eases variant storage, but rank, target modules, quantization, and merge strategy affect quality and serving complexity.
Production reasoning
items: Choose target modules from measured task needs.
Evaluate interference when composing adapters.
Version base model and tokenizer with every adapter.

contentBlocks.text: Weight Examples by Reliability
Weighting can emphasize rare critical slices while downweighting uncertain labels, but uncapped weights let a few examples dominate optimization and destabilize training.
Production reasoning
items: Normalize weights to keep the average near one.
Cap rare-slice boosts and confidence penalties.
Log effective sample weight by slice.

lessons.title: Objectives, Losses, and Learned Behavior
lessons.summary: Connect an optimization target to behavior you actually want.

contentBlocks.text: Objectives, Losses, and Learned Behavior

Supervised loss rewards matching reference tokens, preference losses reward relative choices, and reinforcement optimizes a reward. Each is a proxy, so evaluation must check reward hacking, style imitation, and capability regressions.
Production reasoning
items: Inspect per-slice loss and downstream metrics.
Keep reward and evaluation independently designed.
Test outside the exact training prompt format.

contentBlocks.text: Optimization amplifies whatever the objective measures, including unintended shortcuts.

challenge.instructions: Choose the production-safe answer.

choices.text: Use a task-linked objective and independent slice-aware evaluations.

challenge.explanation: Optimization amplifies whatever the objective measures, including unintended shortcuts.

lessons.title: Detecting Catastrophic Forgetting
lessons.summary: Check specialization does not erase broad capability or safety.

contentBlocks.text: Detecting Catastrophic Forgetting

Fine-tuning can improve a narrow task while degrading instruction following, language coverage, calibration, or refusals. A retention suite compares adapted and base models across representative capabilities and critical constraints.
Production reasoning
items: Use identical harness versions for both checkpoints.
Track absolute quality and regression deltas.
Include out-of-domain behavior that should remain stable.

contentBlocks.text: A specialist gain is unacceptable when it silently removes a critical general capability.

challenge.instructions: Choose the production-safe answer.

choices.text: Gate target-task gains plus retention and safety non-regression.

Ignore all base-task regressions.

challenge.explanation: A specialist gain is unacceptable when it silently removes a critical general capability.
hints: Use identical harness versions for both checkpoints.
Track absolute quality and regression deltas.

lessons.title: Select a Checkpoint Under Constraints
lessons.summary: Choose the best feasible model, not merely lowest validation loss.

contentBlocks.text: Select a Checkpoint Under Constraints
Selection is constrained across target quality, retention, safety, latency, and size. Filter candidates violating hard requirements, then rank remaining models with a documented utility.
Production reasoning
items: Keep safety outside compensating averages.
Normalize comparable soft metrics before weighting.
Record why the winner beat each alternative.

lessons.title: Roll Out an Adapted Model Safely
lessons.summary: Separate promotion from full-traffic exposure.

contentBlocks.text: Roll Out an Adapted Model Safely

A checkpoint should pass offline gates, shadow traffic without acting, serve a small canary, and ramp only while quality, safety, latency, and cost remain bounded. Rollback restores the entire versioned bundle.
Production reasoning
items: Pin adapter, base, tokenizer, prompt, and policy.
Compare canary to concurrent control traffic.
Precompute and test rollback triggers.

contentBlocks.text: A model rollout is a reversible experiment with guardrails.

challenge.instructions: Choose the design preserving invariants under failure.

choices.text: Shadow, canary with controls, then ramp under automatic guardrails.

challenge.explanation: A model rollout is a reversible experiment with guardrails.
hints: Pin adapter, base, tokenizer, prompt, and policy.
Compare canary to concurrent control traffic.

lessons.summary: Turn feedback into candidates without silently harvesting users.

contentBlocks.text: Build a Consent-Aware Data Flywheel

A flywheel needs eligibility rules, privacy filtering, deduplication, review, and lineage from interaction to dataset. Corrections are valuable signals, but consent and deletion must propagate to derived artifacts.
Production reasoning
items: Separate analytics consent from training consent.
Store source IDs for deletion and rebuild.
Sample failures by impact, not frequency alone.

lessons.title: Decompose the Latency Budget
lessons.summary: Measure queueing, prefill, decoding, tools, and network separately.

contentBlocks.text: Decompose the Latency Budget

Users experience time to first token and completion differently. Break total latency into admission, queue, prompt processing, first decode, per-token decode, external calls, and transport so optimization targets the actual bottleneck.
Production reasoning
items: Report p50, p95, and p99 by request class.
Separate compute from queue and network time.
Track prompt and completion lengths with traces.

contentBlocks.text: A lower average can coexist with worse experience when tail queueing grows.

challenge.instructions: Choose the production-safe answer.

choices.text: Instrument each stage and optimize the dominant product percentile.
Report only mean end-to-end latency.

challenge.explanation: A lower average can coexist with worse experience when tail queueing grows.
hints: Report p50, p95, and p99 by request class.
Separate compute from queue and network time.

lessons.title: Continuous and Dynamic Batching
lessons.summary: Trade individual waiting time for accelerator utilization.

contentBlocks.text: Continuous and Dynamic Batching

Batching combines work so matrix operations use hardware efficiently, but waiting too long harms latency. Continuous batching admits new requests as others finish; token-aware schedulers reduce interference between prefill and decode.
Production reasoning
items: Use class-specific queue budgets.
Cap total tokens, not request count alone.
Measure head-of-line blocking from long prompts.

contentBlocks.text: The right batch policy is workload- and SLO-dependent; maximum throughput is not always the objective.

hints: Use class-specific queue budgets.
Cap total tokens, not request count alone.

lessons.title: Schedule Requests by Token Cost
lessons.summary: Prevent one enormous prompt from blocking a queue.

contentBlocks.text: Schedule Requests by Token Cost
A token-aware scheduler estimates prefill and decode work, respects priority, and packs requests within a batch budget. It avoids treating a 50-token query and 50,000-token document as equal work.
Production reasoning
items: Reject work exceeding the configured maximum.
Age requests to prevent starvation.
Reserve capacity for interactive traffic.

lessons.title: Serving Topology for Mixed Workloads
lessons.summary: Isolate traffic classes with incompatible latency and cost profiles.

contentBlocks.text: Serving Topology for Mixed Workloads

Interactive chat, offline extraction, embeddings, and long-context jobs compete differently for memory and compute. Separate pools protect interactive SLOs while a shared gateway owns authentication, quotas, routing, and telemetry.
Production reasoning
items: Route by validated workload class and limits.
Autoscale on queue delay and utilization.
Degrade safely when a specialist pool fails.

lessons.title: Quantization as a Measured Trade-off
lessons.summary: Reduce precision while checking quality, memory, and hardware behavior.

contentBlocks.text: Quantization as a Measured Trade-off

Quantization stores weights or activations with fewer bits, reducing memory bandwidth and sometimes raising throughput. Gains depend on kernel support and model shape; critical slices can lose quality.
Production reasoning
items: Compare end-to-end latency, not only file size.
Evaluate critical slices at each precision.
Measure memory headroom under concurrency.

contentBlocks.text: A smaller checkpoint is not automatically faster when hardware lacks efficient kernels.

hints: Compare end-to-end latency, not only file size.

lessons.title: Overload Control and Load Shedding
lessons.summary: Reject work early enough to preserve useful service.

contentBlocks.text: Overload Control and Load Shedding

When arrivals exceed capacity, queues grow until every request times out. Admission control estimates work, enforces queue and tenant budgets, and sheds low-priority requests with retry guidance before collapse.
Production reasoning
items: Bound queue delay as well as length.
Reserve capacity for health and critical traffic.
Degrade optional features before core responses.

contentBlocks.text: A controlled rejection is better than work that cannot finish before deadline.

contentBlocks.text: Implement a Circuit Breaker
A breaker opens after recent failures, fails fast during cooldown, and becomes half-open for limited probes. It prevents cascading latency without permanently disabling a recovered dependency.

Allow few half-open probes.
Reset only after successful recovery evidence.

lessons.summary: Translate traffic distributions into memory and compute requirements.

contentBlocks.text: Accelerator Capacity Planning

Capacity depends on weights, key-value cache per active token, batch shape, length distributions, target percentiles, and failure headroom. Benchmarks beat peak FLOPS because kernels and memory traffic dominate.

items: Size for percentile concurrency, not averages.
Reserve failover and deployment headroom.
Model prefill and decode separately.

An AI trace connects request class, model and prompt versions, evidence IDs, tool calls, policy decisions, token use, stage latency, and outcome. Raw private text should be minimized, restricted, and retained only as justified.

lessons.title: Privacy-Preserving Traces

contentBlocks.text: Model Routing by Requirement

A router may choose local, small, large, specialist, or cached paths. Remove candidates that violate hard constraints, then rank feasible options by measured quality and cost, with explicit fallback behavior.

lessons.title: Build a Budget-Aware Model Router
lessons.summary: Choose the least expensive feasible route.

contentBlocks.text: Build a Budget-Aware Model Router
Eligibility covers capability, privacy, context, latency, quality, and request budget. Cost cannot compensate for a failed hard constraint, and no match must be explicit.
Production reasoning
items: Separate eligibility from ranking.
Use measured latency percentiles.

contentBlocks.text:
def choose_model(models,request):
    ok=[]
    for m in models:
        if not set(request["capabilities"]).issubset(m["capabilities"]): continue
        if request["privacy"] not in m["privacy_modes"]: continue
        if m["context"]<request["required_context"] or m["p95_ms"]>request["max_ms"]: continue
        if m["quality"]<request["min_quality"] or m["cost"]>request["max_cost"]: continue
        ok.append(m)
    return min(ok,key=lambda m:m["cost"]) if ok else None

Create kill switches for model, retrieval, and side effects.

lessons.title: Implement Permission-Filtered Retrieval
lessons.summary: Filter authorization before candidate text reaches model context.

contentBlocks.text: Implement Permission-Filtered Retrieval
Post-filtering an answer is too late: unauthorized evidence may already influence output or traces. Retrieval enforces tenant and document ACLs before ranking and context assembly.
Production reasoning
items: Apply tenant filters inside the query layer.
Return evidence IDs, versions, scores, and decisions.
